questions.q: Databricks describes three layers for ingestion: Structured Streaming, Lakeflow pipelines and managed connectors. Which layer does Databricks recommend starting with?

options.t: The most managed layer that fits the source, dropping down only if it doesn't
Structured Streaming, because it gives full control and exactly-once guarantees
options.why: It is the most customisable layer, but Databricks recommends starting with the most managed one.

options.t: Lakeflow pipelines always, since managed connectors are only for SaaS sources
options.why: Managed connectors also cover databases, files and streams, and are the recommended starting point where they fit.

options.t: Whichever layer the team already knows, as the three are equivalent
options.why: The layers differ in what they manage for you; the recommendation is to start with the most managed.

questions.explain: Databricks orders the layers from most customisable (Structured Streaming) to most managed (managed connectors) and recommends starting with the most managed layer that fits.

questions.q: A COPY INTO statement loads CSV files from an ADLS folder into a Delta table. It is run again an hour later, and no new files have arrived. What happens?

options.t: Every file is loaded again, duplicating the rows unless the table is truncated first
options.why: COPY INTO skips files it has already loaded; reruns don't duplicate them.

options.t: Nothing is loaded: files already loaded are skipped
The statement fails because the target table already contains the files' rows
options.why: It doesn't fail; it is idempotent and simply loads nothing new.

options.t: Only rows that changed in the files since the first run are merged in
options.why: COPY INTO tracks files, not rows; an already-loaded file is skipped as a whole.

questions.explain: COPY INTO is retriable and idempotent: files already loaded are skipped on later runs, giving exactly-once file processing by default.

questions.q: You want COPY INTO to infer the schema of new JSON files and create the columns in an empty target table. What is the documented approach?

options.t: Create the target with all columns typed as STRING, then run COPY INTO
options.why: Not needed: COPY INTO can infer and merge the schema into an empty placeholder table.

options.t: Run a CREATE TABLE AS SELECT on the files first; COPY INTO can't change a schema
options.why: COPY INTO can infer, merge and evolve the target schema with mergeSchema.

options.t: Create an empty placeholder table, then set mergeSchema in FORMAT_OPTIONS and COPY_OPTIONS
Set the session property spark.databricks.delta.schema.autoMerge.enabled to true and run COPY INTO with no options
options.why: That session setting is legacy; the documented COPY INTO pattern uses mergeSchema in both option lists.

questions.explain: Create an empty table (CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS t;) and set 'mergeSchema' = 'true' in both FORMAT_OPTIONS and COPY_OPTIONS (Databricks Runtime 11.3 LTS and above).

questions.q: Which of these sources can COPY INTO load from?

options.t: Only Unity Catalog volumes; cloud storage paths such as ADLS need Auto Loader instead
options.why: COPY INTO also loads from cloud storage paths such as ADLS (abfss://), S3 and GCS.

options.t: Only Kafka topics and Event Hubs
options.why: COPY INTO loads files; streams need a streaming read.

options.t: Only tables in the legacy Hive metastore
options.why: COPY INTO loads files from a location into a Delta table.

options.t: Files in cloud storage such as ADLS, or in a Unity Catalog volume

questions.explain: COPY INTO loads files from a location (S3, ADLS/ABFS, GCS or a Unity Catalog volume) into a Delta table, in formats including CSV, JSON, XML, Avro, ORC, Parquet, text and binary.

questions.q: A SQL analyst loads new files into a table every hour with COPY INTO. For incremental file loading in SQL, what does Databricks recommend instead?

options.t: A streaming table that reads the files with Auto Loader
A plain INSERT INTO ... SELECT from read_files() every hour
options.why: That reloads every file each time; Databricks recommends streaming tables with Auto Loader for incremental SQL loads.

options.t: A materialized view over read_files(), refreshed hourly
options.why: Databricks names CREATE STREAMING TABLE with Auto Loader as the recommended alternative to COPY INTO.

options.t: A Lakeflow Connect SaaS connector pointed at the folder
options.why: SaaS connectors read SaaS applications; files in storage are read with Auto Loader.

questions.explain: For SQL users loading files incrementally, Databricks recommends CREATE STREAMING TABLE (with Auto Loader) as the recommended alternative to COPY INTO, calling it more scalable and robust.

questions.q: A team needs to ingest a SQL Server database with change data capture into Databricks, with as little custom code as possible. What should they start with?

options.t: A JDBC read in a notebook scheduled every five minutes
options.why: Possible, but you own CDC, retries and schema changes; Databricks recommends the most managed option first.

options.t: Auto Loader pointed at the database's data files
options.why: Auto Loader reads files in cloud storage, not a database.

options.t: COPY INTO with the database's connection string
options.why: COPY INTO loads files from storage locations, not databases.

options.t: A Lakeflow Connect database connector for SQL Server

questions.explain: Lakeflow Connect's database connectors (MySQL, PostgreSQL, Oracle, SQL Server) use change data capture and handle authentication, schema evolution and retries, which is the most managed layer.

questions.q: Which components make up a Lakeflow Connect managed connector for a database source?

options.t: A connection, an ingestion gateway, staging storage, an ingestion pipeline and destination tables
A secret scope with the source password, a JDBC notebook, and an all-purpose cluster that runs it on a schedule
options.why: Managed connectors don't rely on hand-written notebooks; they use a connection, gateway, pipeline and destination tables.

options.t: A storage credential, an external location and a COPY INTO job
options.why: Those are storage-access objects and a file-loading command, not the parts of a database connector.

options.t: A Kafka topic, a schema registry and a streaming sink
options.why: Those belong to event streaming, not to a managed database connector.

questions.explain: A managed connector has a connection (a Unity Catalog securable holding the source credentials), an ingestion pipeline writing streaming tables, and destination tables; database connectors add an ingestion gateway (a continuous job task) and staging storage.

questions.q: After a Lakeflow Connect database connector's first full load, what does it ingest on later runs?

options.t: A complete snapshot of every table on every run, compared with the previous snapshot
options.why: After the first full load, managed connectors ingest only changes.

options.t: Only the changes, using CDC or change tracking where the source supports it
Only new tables added to the source since the last run
options.why: It ingests changed rows of the tables it covers, not only new tables.

options.t: Nothing unless a full refresh is requested
options.why: Incremental change ingestion is what the connector does after the first load.

questions.explain: After the first full load, managed connectors ingest only changes: CDC or change tracking where the source supports it (a cursor column for Salesforce).

questions.q: In a Lakeflow Connect managed connector, what holds the credentials for the source system?

options.t: A notebook widget filled in at run time
options.why: Credentials aren't passed through notebooks; the connector uses a connection object.

options.t: An environment variable set on the ingestion cluster by a workspace admin
options.why: Managed connectors store source credentials in a Unity Catalog connection.

options.t: A storage credential in Unity Catalog
options.why: Storage credentials hold cloud storage credentials; the source's credentials go in a connection.

options.t: A connection, which is a Unity Catalog securable

questions.explain: The connection is a Unity Catalog securable that holds the source credentials, so access to it is governed like any other securable.

questions.q: What does a Lakeflow Connect ingestion pipeline write its data into?

options.t: Streaming tables, on serverless compute by default
Materialized views, recomputed in full on each run
options.why: Managed connectors' ingestion pipelines write streaming tables.

options.t: External Parquet folders that you register afterwards
options.why: They write Unity Catalog streaming tables, not unregistered folders.

options.t: Temporary views that disappear after each run
options.why: The destination tables persist; they are streaming tables.

questions.explain: An ingestion pipeline writes streaming tables, serverless by default, into the destination tables.

questions.q: The exam guide mentions Lakeflow Connect 'standard connectors'. How does the current Databricks documentation describe the non-managed ways to ingest files and streams?

options.t: As 'standard connectors', a separate product tier with its own setup UI and pricing
options.why: The documentation read for this bank doesn't define 'standard connectors'; it describes SQL and Spark APIs.

options.t: As SQL and Spark APIs: Auto Loader, COPY INTO, Kafka and other sources
As partner connectors installed from Partner Connect only
options.why: Partner tools exist, but the documentation's own term for these methods is SQL and Spark APIs.

options.t: As legacy methods that Databricks no longer supports
options.why: Auto Loader and COPY INTO are current, documented ingestion methods.

questions.explain: The documentation uses 'managed connectors' and 'SQL and Spark APIs' (Auto Loader, COPY INTO, Kafka and other sources). It does not define 'standard connectors', the exam guide's term.

questions.q: Which is a benefit managed connectors add on top of Lakeflow pipelines, according to Databricks?

options.t: Exactly-once processing, which pipelines don't provide
options.why: Exactly-once is a property of the lower layers too; connectors add source-specific handling.

options.t: The ability to write Delta tables, which pipelines can't
options.why: Pipelines write Delta tables; that isn't what connectors add.

options.t: Source authentication, CDC, API maintenance, retries and automatic schema evolution
Running only on classic compute in your own VNet, for tighter network control over sources
options.why: Their ingestion pipelines are serverless by default.

questions.explain: Managed connectors are built on pipelines and add source authentication, CDC, handling of edge cases, API maintenance, retries and automatic schema evolution.

questions.q: Events arrive continuously on a Kafka topic and must land in a bronze Delta table within seconds. Which approach fits?

options.t: COPY INTO run every minute against the topic
options.why: COPY INTO loads files from storage locations, not topics.

options.t: Auto Loader with the topic name as its path
options.why: Auto Loader reads files in cloud storage, not Kafka topics.

options.t: A materialized view defined over the Kafka topic and refreshed every hour by a scheduled job
options.why: Hourly refreshes don't meet a latency of seconds, and a topic is read as a stream.

options.t: A streaming read of the topic, as Structured Streaming or a pipeline streaming table

questions.explain: Kafka is a streaming source: read it with Structured Streaming or a streaming table in a pipeline (Lakeflow Connect also lists Kafka among its streaming connectors).

questions.q: Which statements about COPY INTO are true?

options.t: It is idempotent: files already loaded are skipped
It can infer and evolve the target schema with mergeSchema
It reads only from Kafka and Event Hubs
options.why: It loads files from cloud storage and volumes.

options.t: It deletes the source files after loading them
options.why: Nothing in COPY INTO's behaviour deletes source files; it tracks which ones it loaded.

options.t: It requires a Lakeflow pipeline to run
options.why: COPY INTO is a SQL command you can run anywhere SQL runs.

questions.explain: COPY INTO is retriable and idempotent (already-loaded files are skipped) and can infer, merge and evolve the target schema with mergeSchema.

questions.q: Raw JSON events have an array field `items`. In silver you need one row per item. Which function produces that?

options.t: approx_count_distinct(items)
options.why: That estimates a distinct count; it doesn't produce rows.

options.t: explode(items)
dropDuplicates(['items'])
options.why: That removes duplicate rows; it doesn't split an array into rows.

options.t: unionByName(items)
options.why: unionByName combines two DataFrames; it doesn't flatten an array.

questions.explain: explode(col) returns one row per element of an array (or entry of a map), which is how nested JSON arrays are flattened.

questions.q: Databricks suggests how bronze tables should store fields from sources whose schema may change unexpectedly. What is the suggestion?

options.t: Cast every field to its final business type on ingestion so errors surface early
options.why: Strict typing in bronze risks dropping data on schema surprises; typing belongs in silver.

options.t: Store only the fields analysts need and drop the rest
options.why: Bronze keeps the raw state of the source as the base for reprocessing and audit.

options.t: Store most fields as string, VARIANT or binary, plus provenance metadata
Store each record as a separate Parquet file without a table
options.why: Bronze is a table, appended incrementally; loose files lose the guarantees of Delta.

questions.explain: Bronze keeps the source's raw state with minimal validation; Databricks suggests storing most fields as string, VARIANT or binary so schema surprises don't drop data, plus provenance metadata such as the file name.

questions.q: A REST API has no Lakeflow Connect connector. A notebook calls it and appends the results to a bronze table. How should the load be run every night?

options.t: As a task in a Lakeflow job with a scheduled trigger
As a COPY INTO statement pointed at the API URL
options.why: COPY INTO loads files from storage locations, not REST endpoints.

options.t: By leaving the notebook attached to an all-purpose cluster with a sleep loop
options.why: Scheduled work belongs in a job; all-purpose compute isn't recommended for production jobs.

options.t: As an Auto Loader stream with the API as its source path
options.why: Auto Loader reads files in cloud storage, not REST APIs.

questions.explain: Custom ingestion code (JDBC, ODBC or REST clients in notebooks) is scheduled as a Lakeflow job task, here with a scheduled (time-based) trigger.

questions.q: A job must pick up whatever new files arrived since its last run, process them exactly once, and stop. It runs hourly on serverless. Which streaming trigger fits?

options.t: processingTime='1 hour', with the job left running
options.why: Serverless jobs support only availableNow and Once; a continuously running stream isn't the hourly pattern.

options.t: No trigger, so it runs micro-batches continuously
options.why: That runs continuously; serverless notebooks and jobs don't support it.

options.t: Continuous mode
options.why: Continuous mode isn't supported on Databricks.

options.t: availableNow=True

questions.explain: availableNow processes everything available now in micro-batches, then stops: the incremental batch pattern for scheduled jobs, and the trigger serverless jobs support.

questions.q: Which trigger is deprecated and should be replaced by availableNow?

options.t: processingTime
options.why: processingTime is a current trigger for fixed-interval micro-batches.

options.t: Trigger.Once
realTime
options.why: realTime is the trigger for real-time mode, not deprecated.

options.t: The default (unspecified) trigger
options.why: The default trigger is current: a new micro-batch as soon as the previous finishes.

questions.explain: Trigger.Once is deprecated (since Databricks Runtime 11.3 LTS); availableNow replaces it, processing everything available in micro-batches and then stopping.

questions.q: Raw CSV files from a partner must land somewhere governed by Unity Catalog before they are ingested. What is the Unity Catalog object for that?

options.t: A managed table with a single STRING column holding each file's contents
options.why: Files can't be registered as tables this way; volumes hold non-tabular files.

options.t: A schema with no tables
options.why: A schema is a container; the governed object for files is a volume inside it.

options.t: A volume, at /Volumes/<catalog>/<schema>/<volume>/
A storage credential
options.why: A storage credential wraps a cloud credential; it doesn't hold files.

questions.explain: Volumes govern non-tabular files of any format; uses include landing zones for raw files and staging for Auto Loader or COPY INTO.

questions.q: Which sources are listed among Lakeflow Connect's managed connectors?

options.t: Salesforce and Workday
SQL Server and PostgreSQL
Unity Catalog volumes only
options.why: Lakeflow Connect covers databases, SaaS, files and streams, not only volumes.

options.t: The legacy Hive metastore
options.why: The Hive metastore is a metadata store, not an ingestion source of Lakeflow Connect.

options.t: Notebook output cells
options.why: Notebook output isn't an ingestion source.

questions.explain: Lakeflow Connect includes database connectors (MySQL, PostgreSQL, Oracle, SQL Server) and SaaS connectors (Salesforce, HubSpot, Jira, Workday and others), plus file and streaming connectors.
